strengths: Extensive, well-organized empirical evaluation across 48 VRP variants (3x prior work), with consistent improvements over multi-task baselines MTPOMO and MVMoE in Table 1 and materially stronger out-of-distribution generalization (Appendix D.1) and real-world CVRPLIB performance (Table 9: 12.3% avg gap for RF-TE vs. ~18.8% for MVMoE and ~30% for MTPOMO on single-task models).

The unified MDOVRPMBLTW environment is a genuinely useful artifact: its modular attribute switch-on/off design cleanly supports any subset of constraints, correctly adopts the OR-community definition of backhauls/mixed backhauls (App. A), and is fully specified for replication (App. A.2, logic and masks).

The Efficient Adapter Layers (EAL) idea is well-motivated and well-validated: zero-padding new attribute rows preserves zero-shot performance at 'step 0' (Table 2) whereas AL catastrophically degrades it, and EAL consistently beats AL and training-from-scratch in Tables 10-13, with the advantage growing as the fine-tuning task gets harder (MB+MD).
Reproducibility is strong: code is released, hyperparameters are tabulated (Table 4), environment logic and normalization/scaling rules are detailed, and used assets/licenses are disclosed (Table 5).

The component-level analyses are convincing rather than hand-wavy: ablations on transformer components (Fig. 5-7), reward normalization (Fig. 8), MBT stability and imbalanced variants (Fig. 9-11), and t-SNE latent-space interpretability (Fig. 12-13) each isolate the contribution of the proposed pieces.
weaknesses: Several nominally central architectural ingredients (RMSNorm, pre-norm, SwiGLU, FlashAttention) are standard modern-transformer components repurposed from LLM literature rather than original contributions; the novelty rests more on the combination and the training/fine-tuning schemes, and the in-distribution gains over MVMoE in Table 1 are frequently small (often <0.5% absolute gap on n=50).

Presentation problems reduce clarity: the Efficient Adapter Layers weight-matrix equation in Section 4.4 is garbled and hard to parse, Table 9 column alignment looks inconsistent (some 'Obj.' entries for the POMO/MTPOMO/MVMoE blocks appear missing or shifted), and there are assorted typos — these should be fixed.

The 'foundation model' framing is somewhat overstated relative to what is delivered: the system is a multi-task RL solver with an adapter mechanism for fine-tuning, conceptually close to prior multi-task work (MTPOMO, MVMoE, Lin et al.); no large-scale pretraining corpus or scaled model is introduced, and 'foundation' is used loosely.

The RL contributions are relatively simple: Mixed Batch Training amounts to independently sampling attribute activations with probability p_nu per instance, and the reward normalization (Section 4.3.2) is a straightforward mean/EMA subtraction or division; the paper's own ablations (Fig. 5, 8) show reward normalization yields only a marginal improvement.

The paper's claim of 'reducing optimality gaps by more than 10% across all variants' is a relative-improvement framing that can obscure the modest absolute gaps (e.g., many Table 1 entries differ from MVMoE by tenths of a percent); the headline should be qualified.

strengths: The paper delivers a genuinely comprehensive engineering artifact: a unified VRP environment that composes seven attributes and supports many variants, together with extensive experiments (main results plus multiple appendix studies on out-of-distribution attributes, CVRPLIB, encoder ablations, reward normalization, MBT, and t-SNE analysis). This is a useful benchmark/resource contribution.

The Efficient Adapter Layer (EAL) idea (zero-padding new attribute rows in the projection matrices so the pre-trained function is preserved) is simple, sensible, and empirically effective: in Tables 2/10/11/12 EAL finetuning consistently beats AL (Lin et al., 2024) and scratch training on unseen MD/MB variants by a meaningful relative margin.

Reproducibility is handled reasonably well: code is stated to be public, hyperparameters are listed in Table 4, and the unified environment / environment logic are described in detail in the appendix.

The problem setting (transferable/foundation solvers that can be finetuned to new constraints) is practically relevant, and demonstrating finetuning to previously-unmodeled attributes (mixed backhauls, multi-depot) is a worthwhile direction.
weaknesses: The core empirical claim is only marginally supported and is partly contradicted by the authors' own table. In Table 1 (CVRP, n=50) RF-TE has gap 1.274% while MVMoE has 1.242% and RF-MoE 1.226% — i.e., the flagship model does not beat the baselines there, so the statement that RouteFinder "outperforms recent state-of-the-art learning methods" / "in all settings" is not accurate. Most gains are fractions of a percentage point and may be within run-to-run noise, yet no variance/error bars or significance tests are reported.

The abstract's claim of "reducing optimality gaps by more than 10% across all variants" is not supported by the data. For OVRPBLTW (n=50), MTPOMO is 1.260% and RF-TE is 1.150% (well under 10% relative reduction); several other entries are similarly below the claimed threshold. The improvement is stated as a relative gap reduction while the text frames it as an absolute/significant improvement, which is misleading.

The "48 VRP variants" framing is inflated. The main in-distribution evaluation covers a small subset (essentially the MVMoE set); the multi-depot and mixed-backhaul variants are only used in zero-shot/finetuning experiments, where residual gaps remain very large (e.g., 11–19% against HGS in Table 2). This overstates the scope of the contribution.

The headline EAL property — that it "maintains zero-shot performance at step 0" — is trivially true by construction: appending zero-initialized rows leaves the function unchanged. Presenting this as the key empirical advantage over AL (which does change the output distribution) is more a design observation than a research finding, and it is contrasted against AL step-0 in a way that flatters EAL.

Originality is limited. The framework is built directly on the attribute-composition paradigm of Liu et al. (2024a) and Zhou et al. (2024); Global Attribute Embeddings are a straightforward projection of global features onto depot nodes; the Transformer encoder is just an adoption of off-the-shelf modern components (pre-norm, RMSNorm, SwiGLU, FlashAttention); and Mixed Batch Training / reward normalization are simple, well-known tricks. The paper reads largely as careful engineering/tuning rather than a novel methodological advance.

Presentation problems weaken confidence in the results. Table 9 (CVRPLIB) appears misaligned — e.g., X-n502-k39 shows Opt = 69226 and an "MTPOMO" objective also = 69226 but a reported gap of 9.410%, with several columns that do not reconcile. Table 1 also contains duplicate/identical baseline rows (OVRPL and VRPB n=100 have identical HGS-PyVRP/OR-Tools values), which suggests a data-handling error. Dense unaligned tables and column imbalances make the main results hard to verify.

The motivation for a "foundation model" is weak: the model still trails classical heuristics (HGS/PyVRP/OR-Tools) by large margins, including on the very variants it is trained on, and the paper does not convincingly show why the added complexity over MTPOMO/MVMoE is justified given the marginal returns. The limitations discussion is thin, acknowledging the in-distribution quality trade-off only in one sentence.

strengths: The paper provides a unified VRP environment and modular attribute composition that supports a large family of VRP variants, enabling multi-task training and transfer to unseen attributes in a principled way.

The empirical evaluation is extensive: 16 in-distribution synthetic variants, additional zero-shot and finetuning experiments on multi-depot and mixed-backhaul variants, out-of-distribution attribute tests, CVRPLIB large-scale evaluation, and ablations for all proposed components.

RouteFinder consistently improves over MTPOMO and MVMoE, often by meaningful relative margins, e.g., CVRP n=100 gap 3.178% vs 3.788% for MVMoE, CVRPLIB average gap 12.303% vs 18.795% for MVMoE, and large gains in unseen multi-depot/mixed-backhaul finetuning.

The proposed training techniques, Mixed Batch Training and Multi-Variant Reward Normalization, are simple and effective; the ablations and training-curve analyses provide credible evidence that they improve stability and multi-task convergence.

Efficient Adapter Layers are a lightweight and well-motivated finetuning mechanism. The step-0 result is particularly informative: EAL preserves zero-shot performance, whereas standard adapter layers catastrophically degrade it before finetuning.
The paper is generally well written, transparent about architecture and training choices, and includes a detailed hyperparameter table, data-generation description, and licensing information.
The authors provide substantial reproducibility material, including pseudo-code-level environment logic, model equations, hyperparameters, hardware details, and an intention to release code.
weaknesses: The abstract and introduction overclaim that RouteFinder reduces optimality gaps by 'more than 10%' across all variants. Table 1 shows several variants where the relative improvement over MTPOMO/MVMoE is below 10%, and the claim mixes absolute percentage-point gaps with relative reductions.

The abstract advertises experiments on 48 VRP variants, but the main in-distribution results cover a smaller subset; the remaining variants are largely in zero-shot/finetuning appendices. The scope should be described more precisely.

The fairness of the main neural baseline comparison is not fully explicit. It is unclear whether MTPOMO and MVMoE in Table 1 were retrained under the same 300-epoch, all-attribute, unified-environment setup as RouteFinder or taken from prior work; if the latter, the comparison may be confounded.

The technical novelty is moderate rather than fundamental. Attribute composition follows prior work, the transformer changes are largely standard modern LLM components, and EAL is essentially zero-padded adapter initialization. The 'foundation model' framing may overstate the generality of the approach.
Practical performance remains far behind strong OR solvers such as PyVRP/HGS, and large-scale CVRPLIB gaps remain substantial (around 12% average), so real-world deployment claims should be tempered.
Main synthetic experiments are limited to n=50 and n=100, with no systematic scaling study on larger synthetic instances; the large-scale evidence is confined to CVRPLIB in the appendix.

Some model variants are not uniformly dominated by RF-TE; for example, RF-MoE is occasionally better. The claim that RF-TE outperforms other models in 'almost all settings' would benefit from clearer statistical analysis and significance testing.

The limitations discussion is brief and mostly relegated to the conclusion. There is little discussion of failure modes, sensitivity to attribute distributions, compute/environmental cost of training many variants, or negative societal/economic implications of deploying learned solvers.
